result.topic_en: A rule for deciding whether a number B is a quadratic residue of a prime A. It uses a Euclidean-algorithm-like chain of divisions and alternating sums of products of floor halves, illustrated with lattice-point diagrams and worked examples (A=47, B=13; A=23, B=6; A=11, B=2).

Regula elegantissima ad diiudicandum, utrum numerus $\mathfrak{B}$ numeri primi $A$ residuum sit an nonresiduum quadraticum

Sit $A = \mathfrak{b}B + C$
$B = \mathfrak{c}C + D$
$C = \mathfrak{d}D + E$
etc.

$[\tfrac12 A][\tfrac12 B] - [\tfrac12 B][\tfrac12 C] + [\tfrac12 C][\tfrac12 D] - $ etc.

Muss noch hinzukommen
$(\tfrac12 B - 1)(\tfrac14 A + \tfrac14)$

methods.what: Euclidean-algorithm chain of divisions starting from A and B
Alternating sum of products of floor halves plus correction terms, whose parity decides quadratic residuosity
methods.quote:
$[\tfrac12 A][\tfrac12 B] - [\tfrac12 B][\tfrac12 C] + [\tfrac12 C][\tfrac12 D] - $ etc.
$- \tfrac12 \mathfrak{b}[\tfrac12 B]^2 [-+-] + \tfrac12 \mathfrak{c}[\tfrac12 C]^2 - $
$- \tfrac12 \mathfrak{b}[\tfrac12 B] + \tfrac12 \mathfrak{c}[\tfrac12 C] - $ etc. par vel impar

methods.what: Correction term needed to cover even B
Lattice-point reciprocity identity for floor sums (counting points under a diagonal)
Reduction of the floor sum using A = bB + C
Gauss-lemma-type floor sum used as criterion
Worked numerical examples of the rule

items.quote: Regula elegantissima ad diiudicandum, utrum numerus $\mathfrak{B}$ numeri primi $A$ residuum sit an nonresiduum quadraticum
items.english: A most elegant rule for deciding whether the number B is a quadratic residue or non-residue of the prime number A

items.quote:

$(\tfrac12 B - 1)(\tfrac14 A + \tfrac14)$
um auch die geraden $B$ zu umfassen
items.english: Must still be added: (1/2 B − 1)(1/4 A + 1/4), in order to cover the even B as well
